replacement: “I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, when she chooses to come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”
And he kissed his hand with a smack.
The boys looked at one another as though in mockery.

“Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my point clearer. As for the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I’ll say nothing about them. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, knowing they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. All I know, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian mind, is that there is suffering and nobody is guilty; that cause follows effect plainly and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know it, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that nobody is guilty, that cause follows effect plainly and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I’ll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and place, but here on earth, where I can see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again. If it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer just so that my crimes and my sufferings could manure the ground for somebody else’s future harmony. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion in the world is built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I say it: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer in order to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all understanding why they should suffer, and why they should have to pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity among men in sin. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth does not belong to this world, and I can’t comprehend it. Some jester will say, perhaps, that the child would have grown up and sinned. But he didn’t grow up, you see. He was torn to pieces by dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I do understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will have been reached and everything will be clear. But this is exactly where I stop: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, perhaps it really may happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too, perhaps, may cry out with the rest, as I watch the mother embrace her child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it out then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I renounce the higher harmony altogether. It isn’t worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with her unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn’t worth it, because those tears are unatoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the suffering of children goes to make up the sum of suffering needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who threw her son to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the suffering of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She must not forgive the torturer, even if the child forgave him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I’d rather keep my unavenged suffering. I’d rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, the price of harmony is too high. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to hand it back as soon as I can. That’s what I’m doing. It isn’t God I don’t accept, Alyosha. I just most respectfully return Him the ticket.”

“‘When they receive bread from us, they will see plainly that we take the bread their own hands have made, only to hand it back to them, and that there is no miracle in it. They will see that we do not turn stones into bread. Yet in truth they will be more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! They will remember only too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they came back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. Too, too well will they understand the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame that they do not? Speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures, which is what they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them in the end not to be proud, because You lifted them up and so taught them pride. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children, and that a child’s happiness is the sweetest there is. They will grow timid. They will look to us and press close to us in fear, as chicks do to the hen. They will marvel at us and stand in awe of us. They will take pride in our being so powerful and so clever that we could tame a flock this unruly, thousands of millions strong. They will tremble helplessly before our wrath, their minds will fill with fear, and they will cry as easily as women and children do. But at a sign from us they will turn just as readily to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their free hours we shall arrange their life like a child’s game, with children’s songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall even let them sin. They are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we let them sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for if it is done with our permission. We let them sin because we love them, we shall say, and the punishment for these sins we take on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as the saviors who have borne their sins before God. They will keep no secrets from us. We shall permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, and to have children or not, depending on whether they have obeyed or disobeyed, and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience, all, all of them, they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for all. They will be glad to believe our answer, for it will spare them the great anxiety and the terrible agony they suffer now, having to decide freely for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken on themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall tempt them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for such as they. It is prophesied that You will come again in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and the strong. But we will say that they have saved only themselves, and we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the _mystery_ in her hands, will be put to shame; that the weak will rise up again, tear her royal purple, and strip her loathsome body bare. But then I will stand up and show You the thousand millions of happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins on ourselves for their happiness, will stand before You and say: “Judge us, if You can and dare.” Know that I do not fear You. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom You have blessed men with, and that I too was struggling to take my place among Your elect, among the strong and mighty, hungering “to make up the number.” But I woke up, and I refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Your work_. I left the proud and returned to the humble, for the happiness of the humble. What I tell You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I repeat, tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, which at one sign from me will rush to pile the glowing coals around the stake where I shall burn You for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I shall burn You. _Dixi._’”
